docs.title: Text4GCN
docs.text:
A Python framework for text classification using Graph Neural Networks.

Text4GCN converts a collection of text documents into a word-document graph and trains a Graph Convolutional Network (GCN) on it for document classification. The graph captures vocabulary co-occurrence patterns that traditional bag-of-words models miss.

Scope and limitations

  • Scientific niche: text-graph construction and TGCN with Related Word Filter (RWF) — fewer edges / less memory, accuracy ≈ classic TextGCN (Pereira & de Castro, DCAI 2022). Not a drop-in replacement for fine-tuned transformers on short-text SOTA.
  • Transductive learning: test documents are included in the graph at construction time (same as Yao et al., AAAI 2019). New documents require rebuilding the graph and retraining.
  • Default protocol: dropout 0.5, lr 0.02, hidden 200, early stopping 10, 10% of train as validation via TextPipeline.execute(validation_ratio=0.10).

docs.title: How it works
docs.text: The pipeline has three steps: preprocess text → build the graph → train the GCN. Each step writes files to disk so you can resume at any stage.

docs.title: Key features
docs.text:
• Three adjacency strategies — frequency (TF-IDF/PMI), semantic (Word2Vec, BERT, cosine similarity), syntactic (dependency parsing, LIWC)
  • Graph refinement — filter low-frequency words, prune weak edges, attach node metadata
  • Automatic device selection — detects CUDA, falls back to CPU transparently
  • Structured results — GNN.fit() returns a TrainingResult with test accuracy and loss, macro/weighted metrics, the best epoch and checkpoint path, the per-epoch history, a per-class report and the confusion matrix
  • Informative errors — if a pipeline step is missing, the error shows the exact command to fix it

docs.title: Quick start
docs.text:
pip install text4gcn
pip install "text4gcn[syntactic]"   # optional: Stanford CoreNLP wrapper (Java jars still required)

from text4gcn import GNN, TextPipeline
from text4gcn.builder import Frequency

# Step 1 — preprocess raw text (validation split + shuffle seed live here)
TextPipeline(dataset_name="R8", dataset_path="data/", seed=1234).execute(
    validation_ratio=0.10,
)

# Step 2 — build the word-document graph (returns edge/memory stats)
stats = Frequency(dataset_name="R8", dataset_path="data/").tfidf()
print(stats)  # GraphBuildStats: nodes, edges(nnz), density, file size

# Step 3 — train and evaluate
result = GNN(dataset_name="R8", dataset_path="data/", seed=1234).fit()
print(f"Test accuracy: {result.test_accuracy:.4f}")

Learn by example

The tutorials tell the whole story in five notebooks: from a twelve-sentence graph you can see, to a real benchmark, to comparing graph builders, to your own corpus.

Reproduce DCAI 2022 Tables 2/3 (reference + optional local comparison):

python scripts/reproduce_dcai2022.py --reference-only
python scripts/reproduce_dcai2022.py --data-dir data/ --dataset R8 --builders frequency,semantic

docs.title: Changelog
docs.text: All notable changes to this project are documented here. Format follows Keep a Changelog.

docs.title: Added
docs.text:
• Console output redesigned: one summary line per stage, a progress bar while training and on the slow graph-building steps, and a per-class table at the end; verbose=0/1/2 on TextPipeline, the builders and GNN
  • TrainingResult.best_epoch, metrics, history, report and confusion_matrix (pandas, with class names); GraphBuildStats.word_word_edges and summary()
  • text4gcn.set_verbosity() and TEXT4GCN_VERBOSITY for diagnostic logs, through the standard logging module (NullHandler by default)
  • Tutorials: five notebooks in docs/tutorials/ (text as a graph → first classifier on 20 Newsgroups → comparing graph builders → refining the graph → your own corpus), rendered in the docs with mkdocs-jupyter
  • text4gcn.datasets.save_corpus() writes any labelled corpus in the .txt / .meta input format, with validation
  • text4gcn.datasets.twenty_newsgroups() downloads 20 Newsgroups (scikit-learn) in the input format
  • dataset_path accepts pathlib.Path as well as str (TextPipeline, builders, GNN, datasets)
  • Builder.Bert selects the Semantic.bert() graph in GNN
  • GraphBuildStats returned by every builder method (nodes, nnz, density, file size)
  • TextPipeline(seed=…) for reproducible corpus shuffle
  • Optional text4gcn[syntactic] extra (Stanford CoreNLP Python wrapper) and text4gcn[bert] extra (transformers, for the BERT builder)
  • scripts/reproduce_dcai2022.py for DCAI 2022 Tables 2/3 reference + local comparison
  • MkDocs + Material theme documentation; CI builds with mkdocs build --strict
  • Graph refinement (RefinementConfig, apply_refinement, NodeMetadata)
  • GNN.fit() returns TrainingResult; early-stop restores best validation weights

docs.title: Changed
docs.text:
• TrainingResult is a frozen dataclass and model_path is always set; Semantic.cosine_similarity() and its builder class share the 0.95 default
  • TextPipeline downloads the NLTK resources only when they are missing, quietly
  • Requires PyTorch ≥ 2.3 (earlier builds cannot run with NumPy 2)
  • transformers is no longer installed by default: it is only needed by Semantic.bert(), via the bert extra
  • Training seed is deterministic (GNN(seed=…) seeds torch / NumPy / Python); no random offset
  • Dropout from GNN(dropout=…) is passed into the GCN; model.train() after each eval epoch
  • Semantic.word2vec(threshold=…) defaults to 0.7 instead of 0.95: with the 20 epochs now actually applied, 0.95 left almost no word–word edges (79 on 20 Newsgroups, 4 categories)
  • RWF word–word weights are the pair count divided by the largest pair count, in (0, 1]; PMI is a gate only. (A Max–Min scaling gave the least frequent pairs weight 0, which deleted their edges.)
  • Layer is str, Enum with only Layer.GCN (GAT removed from the public API)
  • CoreNLP import is lazy; syntactic builders require the optional extra
  • Documentation CI uses MkDocs (replacing Sphinx)
  • Development tooling: Ruff replaces black / isort / flake8; one CI workflow lints, tests on Python 3.10–3.13 and builds the package; publishing to PyPI checks that the release tag matches the package version and runs the tests first
  • Corpus is read as UTF-8 by default (was Latin-1); all intermediate files are written/read as UTF-8 regardless of OS locale
  • datasets.download(name, path) replaces data.R8() / R52() / AG_NEWS(): R8, R52, Ohsumed and PubMed from the datasets-v1 GitHub release, with SHA-256 verification (the old Azure storage is gone)

docs.title: Migrating from 1.x
docs.text:
• Requires Python ≥ 3.10 (1.x targeted Python 3.8)
  • No argparse is involved anymore: GNN works in notebooks/Colab (fixes #3)
  • GNN(dataset=…, path=…, epoches=…) → GNN(dataset_name=…, dataset_path=…, epochs=…)
  • builder is optional (default Builder.Tfidf) (fixes #2); Builder.Embedding / Builder.Frequency → Builder.Word2Vec / Builder.Tfidf
  • Import from the package root: from text4gcn import GNN, TextPipeline, Builder, Layer
  • Builder values changed ('frequency' → 'frequency.tfidf', 'embedding' → 'embedding.word2vec', 'cosine' → 'cosine.similarity', 'dependency' → 'dependency.parsing'), and so did the adjacency file names: graphs built with 1.x are not found; build them again
  • Graph files are no longer interchangeable with 1.x even for the same builder: Word2Vec, LIWC, cosine-similarity and RWF weights changed (see Fixed)

docs.title: Removed
docs.text:
• The custom modules.logger (PrintLog, Process), graph.report_stats() and models.show_metrics(): progress goes through verbose, results through the returned objects, diagnostics through logging. tabulate is no longer a dependency
  • output_path of tfidf(), word2vec() and cosine_similarity(), and TextPipeline.execute(use_predefined_word_vectors=…): they were accepted but ignored
  • GNN(val_ratio=…): it never changed the split; set it with TextPipeline.execute(validation_ratio=…)
  • Syntactic.constituency_parsing(), Semantic.llm() and Builder.ConstituencyParsing, which did nothing
  • builder.list_available_adjacency_methods() / list_available_builders() and the string constants builder.Tfidf, builder.Word2Vec, …: use the Builder enum. text4gcn.builder.Builder is now the same enum as text4gcn.Builder (they were two distinct classes); rich is no longer a dependency
  • Unused internal modules (preprocess.DataShuffler, NodeFeatureBuilder, WordProcessor, modules.utils, and empty or unreachable files); the TextPipeline covers what they did
  • The empty cpu and gpu extras: pip install text4gcn installs PyTorch from PyPI; for another build install PyTorch first from pytorch.org
  • utils.recommend_installation(), and the torch_available key of check_pytorch_installation() (PyTorch is a required dependency)
  • data.AG_NEWS() (no longer hosted)
  • Unused models.utils.get_train_test() / read_file()
  • The unfinished baseline models (models/baseline: TF-IDF, LSTM)

docs.title: Fixed
docs.text:
• After graph refinement, the train / test block sizes counted only the training mask, so validation documents were reported as words
  • A document left empty by cleaning produced NaN node features (and a RuntimeWarning); it now gets a zero vector
  • The training log's "Data statistics" table labelled the node count as "Edges"
  • Semantic.word2vec(num_epochs=…) was never passed to gensim, which always trained 5 epochs. Training is now also reproducible: seed (default 1234) and workers (default 1) are new parameters, and vector initialisation no longer depends on PYTHONHASHSEED. The code behind the DCAI 2022 paper had the same bug, so its SEMANTIC results were obtained with 5 epochs
  • Syntactic.linguistic_inquiry() looked words up in the LIWC dictionary letter by letter, so real words never matched; it now connects adjacent words that share at least one LIWC category. The code behind the DCAI 2022 paper had the same bug, so its LINGUISTIC results do not reflect LIWC categories
  • Semantic.cosine_similarity(): words without a WordNet definition all received the same placeholder vector and formed a clique (99% of the word–word edges on 20 Newsgroups); they now get no word–word edges
  • RefinementConfig(keep_docs=True) did not protect documents from min_degree / max_degree
  • RefinementConfig(keep_word_indices=…) now overrides the other word filters, as documented
  • RefinementConfig(top_k_edges_per_node=…) doubled the weight of edges kept by both endpoints
  • Ohsumed's training split (and 20news-bydate-train) was dropped by the shuffle step, which only accepted values ending in train; split handling now follows the documented rule (train, training, 20news-bydate-train → train, anything else → test)
  • RefinementConfig(min_doc_freq=…) / max_doc_freq_ratio counted 0 documents for every word on CSR graphs, which removed all words (chance-level accuracy)
  • Semantic.cosine_similarity() compares word vectors in vectorised chunks (seconds instead of hours on a 10k-word vocabulary) and returns GraphBuildStats like the other builders
  • Training on CUDA: adjacency, masks and predictions now follow the selected device
  • Non-ASCII corpora: TextPipeline(encoding=…, ascii_only=False) keeps words of any script, e.g. Arabic with diacritics (fixes #1)
  • Dataset downloads no longer save HTTP error pages as data
  • apply_refinement CSR conversion before fancy indexing (dia_matrix safe)
  • Early path validation when dataset_path / dataset_name are missing or empty, in TextPipeline, the builders and GNN
  • Builders: the constructors raise ValueError for an empty dataset_name and FileNotFoundError for a missing dataset_path; every builder method raises FileNotFoundError with the TextPipeline command when {dataset_name}.shuffled/ is missing
  • GNN.fit() checks the adjacency file of the selected builder (ind.<builder>.<dataset>.adj), not only the .adjacency/ directory, and its error names the builder call that writes it
  • Labels containing spaces in .meta: label columns are split on tabs only, so a label like "real estate" is no longer truncated
  • Syntactic.dependency_parsing() did not filter stop words: words are now read from the token indices of each dependency relation (ROOT skipped), so language selects the stop-word list
  • np.bool → bool (NumPy ≥ 1.24)

docs.title: Added
docs.text:

docs.text:
Text4GCN requires Python ≥ 3.10 and PyTorch ≥ 2.3. PyTorch comes from PyPI with the package: CUDA-enabled on Linux, CPU-only on Windows and macOS. For another build, install PyTorch first from pytorch.org; see Device Management.

docs.title: Data format
docs.text:
Each dataset needs two files in the same directory:

{dataset_name}.txt — one document per line, UTF-8 by default (pass TextPipeline(encoding="latin1"), or another encoding, for other files): 

computer software engineering systems design
natural language processing machine learning algorithms

{dataset_name}.meta — tab-separated: index split label (labels may contain spaces, not tabs): 

0   train   technology
1   train   science
2   test    technology

Supported split values: train, training, 20news-bydate-train, anything else is treated as test.

Cleaning keeps only ASCII letters and digits by default, as in the original TextGCN; pass TextPipeline(ascii_only=False) to keep non-ASCII letters (accented Latin, Cyrillic, Arabic, …).

docs.title: Get a dataset
docs.text:
from text4gcn.datasets import download, save_corpus, twenty_newsgroups

download("R8", "data/")                       # R8, R52, ohsumed or pubmed (SHA-256 verified)
twenty_newsgroups("data/", name="20NG4",      # via scikit-learn, official train/test split
                  categories=["alt.atheism", "soc.religion.christian", "comp.graphics", "sci.med"])
save_corpus("data/", "mine",                  # your own texts, labels and train/test splits
            texts=["great movie", "boring plot"], labels=["pos", "neg"], splits=["train", "test"])

See the Datasets API and the Bring your own corpus tutorial.

docs.title: Step 1 — Preprocess text
docs.text:
TextPipeline cleans the corpus, shuffles train/test splits, builds a vocabulary, and extracts node feature matrices. Output is written to disk under {dataset_path}/.

from text4gcn import TextPipeline

TextPipeline(
    dataset_name="R8",
    dataset_path="data/",
    rare_count=5,       # drop words appearing fewer than 5 times
    language="english", # language for stop-word removal
    seed=1234,
).execute(validation_ratio=0.10)

After this step the following directories are created:

data/
  R8.cleaned/          ← stop-word and rare-word filtered corpus
  R8.shuffled/         ← train/test splits, vocabulary, word vectors
  R8.node_features/    ← x, y, tx, ty, allx, ally (pickle files)
  log/                 ← pipeline execution log

docs.title: Step 2 — Build the graph
docs.text:
Choose an adjacency strategy that fits your data and compute time budget. See Choosing a Builder for a comparison.

TF-IDF (recommended start)Word2VecBERTCosine similarity 
from text4gcn.builder import Frequency

stats = Frequency(dataset_name="R8", dataset_path="data/").tfidf(window_size=20)
print(stats)  # GraphBuildStats

from text4gcn.builder import Semantic

Semantic(dataset_name="R8", dataset_path="data/").word2vec(
    training_algorithm=1,   # 1 = skip-gram, 0 = CBOW
    embedding_dimension=300,
    num_epochs=20,
    threshold=0.7,
)

from text4gcn.builder import Semantic

Semantic(dataset_name="R8", dataset_path="data/").bert(threshold=0.95)

from text4gcn.builder import Semantic

Semantic(dataset_name="R8", dataset_path="data/").cosine_similarity(threshold=0.9)

After this step:

data/
  R8.adjacency/
    ind.frequency.tfidf.R8.adj   ← serialised scipy sparse matrix

docs.title: Step 3 — Train the GCN
docs.text:
from text4gcn import GNN, Builder

result = GNN(
    dataset_name="R8",
    dataset_path="data/",
    log_dir="logs/",
    builder=Builder.Tfidf,
    seed=1234,
    epochs=200,
    lr=0.02,
    nhid=200,
    dropout=0.5,
    early_stopping=10,
).fit()

print(result)
# TrainingResult(accuracy=0.9712, macro_f1=0.9301, loss=0.0984, epochs=187, best_epoch=177, model_path='logs/…pth')

fit() shows a progress bar while training and ends with a summary: accuracy, macro-F1 and a per-class table. The same numbers are in the result (result.metrics, result.report, result.confusion_matrix, and result.history per epoch). Pass verbose=0 to silence it, or verbose=2 for one line per epoch. Accuracy and loss plots are saved to log_dir/.

Validation ratio

The train/val split is set by TextPipeline.execute(validation_ratio=…) (default 10% of the training documents).

docs.title: Minimal usage
docs.text:
All parameters except dataset_name and dataset_path have sensible defaults:

from text4gcn import GNN

result = GNN(dataset_name="R8", dataset_path="data/", seed=1234).fit()
print(f"accuracy={result.test_accuracy:.4f}")

Defaults: builder=Builder.Tfidf, log_dir=".", epochs=200, lr=0.02, nhid=200, dropout=0.5, early_stopping=10, layer=Layer.GCN, seed=1234, device=None (auto-detect), verbose=1.

docs.title: With graph refinement
docs.text:
Reduce graph size and noise before training:

from text4gcn import GNN, Builder, RefinementConfig

result = GNN(
    dataset_name="R8",
    dataset_path="data/",
    builder=Builder.Tfidf,
    refinement_config=RefinementConfig(
        min_doc_freq=2,              # drop words in fewer than 2 documents
        min_word_degree=1.0,         # drop words whose edge weights sum to < 1
        edge_weight_threshold=0.1,   # drop very weak edges
        keep_docs=True,              # always preserve document nodes
    ),
).fit()

See Graph Refinement for the full parameter reference.

docs.title: Error messages
docs.text:
If you call GNN.fit() without running a previous step, you get an actionable error:

FileNotFoundError: Node feature files not found at 'data/R8.node_features'.

Run the preprocessing step first:

  from text4gcn import TextPipeline
  TextPipeline(
      dataset_name='R8',
      dataset_path='data/',
  ).execute()

A missing graph names the builder call that writes it:

FileNotFoundError: Adjacency file not found at 'data/R8.adjacency/ind.embedding.word2vec.R8.adj'.

Build the 'embedding.word2vec' graph after preprocessing:

  from text4gcn.builder import Semantic
  Semantic(
      dataset_name='R8',
      dataset_path='data/',
  ).word2vec(training_algorithm=1, embedding_dimension=300, num_epochs=20)

The builders raise the same kind of error, with the TextPipeline command, when {dataset_path}/{dataset_name}.shuffled/ is missing.

docs.text:
All public classes and functions are importable directly from the text4gcn top-level package.

    GNN,
    TextPipeline,
    Builder,
    Layer,
    GraphBuildStats,
    RefinementConfig,
    TextGCNTrainer,
    TrainingResult,
    apply_refinement,
    compute_adjacency_stats,
    load_adjacency_stats,
    set_verbosity,
)

Builder classes live in text4gcn.builder:

docs.title: Output and diagnostics
docs.text:
Text4GCN separates three kinds of output, as most current ML libraries do:

What Where Controlled by Progress and summaries of each step printed to stdout verbose= of TextPipeline, the builders and GNN: 0 silent, 1 (default) progress bars and summaries, 2 no progress bars (see below) Results returned objects: TrainingResult (metrics, per-class report, confusion matrix, per-epoch history) and GraphBuildStats — Diagnostics: array shapes, model structure, file details the standard logging module, logger "text4gcn" text4gcn.set_verbosity(...) or your own logging configuration

verbose per class (any other value raises ValueError):

Class 1 (default) 2 TextPipeline One summary line per stage (no progress bars) Same as 1 Frequency / Semantic / Syntactic Header, a progress bar during slow steps, summary line Header and summary line, no progress bar GNN Progress bar over the epochs, then the summary One line per epoch instead of the bar, then the summary

docs.title: Diagnostics
docs.text:
The "text4gcn" logger has only a NullHandler, so it is quiet unless you ask for it:

import text4gcn

text4gcn.set_verbosity("debug")    # "debug", "info", "warning", "error", "critical"

set_verbosity also accepts a logging level number (e.g. logging.DEBUG); an unknown name raises ValueError.

set_verbosity sends the library's messages to stderr; the environment variable TEXT4GCN_VERBOSITY=debug does the same at import time. If your application already configures logging, the text4gcn loggers follow that configuration instead.

docs.title: Builders
docs.text:
from text4gcn.builder import Frequency, Semantic, Syntactic

Builders compute the adjacency matrix — the edges of the word-document graph — from the preprocessed corpus. Run a builder after TextPipeline and before GNN.

docs.title: Builder (enum)
docs.text:
from text4gcn import Builder

Selects which adjacency file GNN loads at training time. Builder is a str enum, so GNN(builder=...) also accepts the plain value (e.g. "embedding.word2vec").

Value Adjacency file prefix Built by Builder.Tfidf frequency.tfidf Frequency(...).tfidf() Builder.Word2Vec embedding.word2vec Semantic(...).word2vec() Builder.Bert embedding.bert Semantic(...).bert() Builder.CosineSimilarity cosine.similarity Semantic(...).cosine_similarity() Builder.DependencyParsing dependency.parsing Syntactic(...).dependency_parsing() Builder.Liwc liwc Syntactic(...).linguistic_inquiry()

docs.title: Frequency
docs.text:
from text4gcn.builder import Frequency

Builds a TF-IDF–weighted word-document graph. Fastest option; recommended as a starting point.

The constructors of Frequency, Semantic and Syntactic raise ValueError if dataset_name is empty or verbose is not 0, 1 or 2, and FileNotFoundError if dataset_path does not exist. Every builder method raises FileNotFoundError, with the TextPipeline command to run, if {dataset_path}/{dataset_name}.shuffled/ is missing.

class Frequency:
    def __init__(self, dataset_name: str, dataset_path: str | os.PathLike[str], verbose: int = 1) -> None

docs.title: tfidf()
docs.text:
def tfidf(self, window_size: int = 20) -> GraphBuildStats

Computes word-word co-occurrence weights via PMI in a sliding window, and word-document weights via TF-IDF. Writes ind.frequency.tfidf.{dataset_name}.adj to {dataset_path}/{dataset_name}.adjacency/.

docs.title: Parameters
docs.text: Parameter Type Default Description window_size int 20 Sliding window size for word-word co-occurrence.

docs.title: Returns
docs.text: GraphBuildStats — node/edge counts, density, and optional file size.

docs.title: Example
docs.text:
from text4gcn.builder import Frequency

stats = Frequency(dataset_name="R8", dataset_path="data/").tfidf(window_size=20)
print(stats)

docs.title: Semantic
docs.text:
from text4gcn.builder import Semantic

Builds edges based on semantic similarity between words (Word2Vec, BERT, cosine similarity).

class Semantic:
    def __init__(self, dataset_name: str, dataset_path: str | os.PathLike[str], verbose: int = 1) -> None

docs.title: word2vec()
docs.text:
def word2vec(
    self,
    training_algorithm: int,
    embedding_dimension: int,
    num_epochs: int,
    language: str = "english",
    threshold: float = 0.7,
    seed: int = 1234,
    workers: int = 1,
) -> GraphBuildStats

Trains Word2Vec embeddings on the corpus and connects adjacent words whose cosine similarity is at least threshold and whose PMI is positive (DCAI Related Word Filter semantic path). Stop words get no edges; the edge weight is the pair count divided by the largest pair count.

docs.title: Parameters
docs.text: Parameter Type Default Description training_algorithm int — 1 = skip-gram (as in the DCAI 2022 paper), 0 = CBOW. embedding_dimension int — Embedding size (e.g. 300). num_epochs int — Word2Vec training epochs (the paper uses 20). language str "english" NLTK stop-word list; stop words get no word–word edges. threshold float 0.7 Minimum cosine similarity between two adjacent words' embeddings to create an edge. Calibrated on 20 Newsgroups: with 20 epochs, the paper's 0.95 leaves almost no word–word edges. seed int 1234 Seed of the Word2Vec initialisation. workers int 1 Word2Vec threads. With 1 the graph is reproducible for a given seed; more threads train faster but vary between runs.

docs.title: Returns
docs.text: GraphBuildStats

docs.title: Example
docs.text:
from text4gcn.builder import Semantic

stats = Semantic(dataset_name="R8", dataset_path="data/").word2vec(
    training_algorithm=1,   # skip-gram
    embedding_dimension=300,
    num_epochs=20,
    threshold=0.7,
)

docs.title: bert()
docs.text:
def bert(self, language: str = "english", threshold: float = 0.95) -> GraphBuildStats

Embeds each vocabulary word on its own with bert-base-uncased (its [CLS] vector, out of sentence context) and, like word2vec(), connects adjacent non-stop-word words whose cosine similarity is at least threshold and whose PMI is positive. The edge weight is the pair count divided by the largest pair count.

Requirements

bert() needs pip install "text4gcn[bert]" and always uses bert-base-uncased, downloaded on first use. Train on its graph with GNN(..., builder=Builder.Bert).

docs.title: Parameters
docs.text: Parameter Type Default Description language str "english" NLTK stop-word list. The model is always bert-base-uncased. threshold float 0.95 Minimum cosine similarity to create an edge.

docs.title: Example
docs.text:
from text4gcn.builder import Semantic

Semantic(dataset_name="R8", dataset_path="data/").bert(threshold=0.95)

docs.title: cosine_similarity()
docs.text:
def cosine_similarity(self, threshold: float = 0.95) -> GraphBuildStats

Connects words whose WordNet definitions are similar: the cosine similarity of the TF-IDF vectors of their glosses, saved by TextPipeline. The edge weight is that similarity. Every word with a vector also gets a self-loop (its similarity with itself is 1, above any threshold below 1), counted in word_word_edges. Words without a WordNet definition get no word–word edges, so the builder is meaningful for English only.

docs.title: Parameters
docs.text: Parameter Type Default Description threshold float 0.95 An edge needs a similarity strictly greater than this.

docs.title: Example
docs.text:
from text4gcn.builder import Semantic

Semantic(dataset_name="R8", dataset_path="data/").cosine_similarity(threshold=0.90)

docs.text:
from text4gcn.builder import Syntactic

Builds edges from syntactic structure: dependency parsing or LIWC categories.

class Syntactic:
    def __init__(self, dataset_name: str, dataset_path: str | os.PathLike[str], verbose: int = 1) -> None

docs.title: dependency_parsing()
docs.text:
def dependency_parsing(self, core_nlp_path: str, language: str = "english") -> GraphBuildStats

Connects words that have a syntactic dependency relation in the corpus, using Stanford CoreNLP. Each relation except ROOT between two non-stop-word words counts as a pair; as in the other RWF builders, a pair needs positive PMI and its weight is the pair count divided by the largest pair count.

Experimental

Needs pip install "text4gcn[syntactic]" and a local Stanford CoreNLP installation (Java jars), which CI does not run. CoreNLP always parses English; language selects the NLTK stop-word list whose words get no edges.

docs.title: Parameters
docs.text: Parameter Type Default Description core_nlp_path str — Path to the CoreNLP installation directory. language str "english" NLTK stop-word list. CoreNLP always parses English.

docs.title: linguistic_inquiry()
docs.text:
def linguistic_inquiry(self, liwc_path: str) -> GraphBuildStats

Connects adjacent words that share at least one LIWC (Linguistic Inquiry and Word Count) category, gated by positive PMI. The edge weight is the pair count divided by the largest pair count.

LIWC dictionary

The LIWC dictionary is proprietary and not distributed with Text4GCN; pass the path to your own .dic file.

docs.title: Parameters
docs.text: Parameter Type Default Description liwc_path str — Path to the LIWC dictionary file.

docs.title: Output layout
docs.text:
All builders write to the same directory:

data/
  R8.adjacency/
    ind.frequency.tfidf.R8.adj        ← Frequency.tfidf()
    ind.embedding.word2vec.R8.adj     ← Semantic.word2vec()
    ind.embedding.bert.R8.adj         ← Semantic.bert()
    ind.cosine.similarity.R8.adj      ← Semantic.cosine_similarity()
    ind.dependency.parsing.R8.adj     ← Syntactic.dependency_parsing()
    ind.liwc.R8.adj                   ← Syntactic.linguistic_inquiry()

The adjacency file is a serialised scipy.sparse matrix. The Builder enum value determines which file GNN loads at training time.

docs.title: GraphBuildStats
docs.text:
from text4gcn import GraphBuildStats

Frozen dataclass returned by every builder method (tfidf(), word2vec(), cosine_similarity(), bert(), dependency_parsing(), linguistic_inquiry()).

Field Type Description n_nodes int Train docs + vocabulary + test docs. n_edges int Number of stored non-zeros (nnz). density float nnz / n_nodes². file_bytes int \| None Pickled adjacency size on disk, if known. builder str \| None Builder label (e.g. frequency.tfidf). dataset_name str \| None Dataset name. path str \| None Path to the adjacency file. word_word_edges int \| None Stored non-zeros between two word nodes. The builders differ only in these: all keep the same TF-IDF document–word edges.

print(stats) shows every field with exact counts:

GraphBuildStats(builder='frequency.tfidf', dataset='20NG4', nodes=14,537, edges=…, word_word=…, density=2.15%, size='52.0 MiB')

stats.summary() returns the short form, a plain string:

14,537 nodes · 4.53 M edges (4.26 M word–word) · density 2.15% · 52.0 MiB

stats.to_dict() returns the fields as a dict (e.g. for a pandas.DataFrame of several builds).

The builders print that summary under a header line (builder console output, verbose=1 or 2):

text4gcn · Frequency.tfidf("20NG4") · window 20
  ✓ graph     14,537 nodes · 4.53 M edges (4.26 M word–word) · density 2.15% · 52.0 MiB  (4m00s)

verbose (0, 1 default, 2) is given to Frequency, Semantic or Syntactic: 0 is silent, 1 prints the header and summary and adds a progress bar during the slow steps (PMI, word pairs), 2 prints the header and summary without the progress bar. The same lines are appended to {dataset_path}/log/{dataset_name}_dataset.txt.

docs.title: compute_adjacency_stats() / load_adjacency_stats()
docs.text:
from text4gcn import compute_adjacency_stats, load_adjacency_stats

def compute_adjacency_stats(
    adj: scipy.sparse.spmatrix,
    *,
    path: str | Path | None = None,
    builder: str | None = None,
    dataset_name: str | None = None,
    word_word_edges: int | None = None,
) -> GraphBuildStats

def load_adjacency_stats(
    path: str | Path,
    *,
    builder: str | None = None,
    dataset_name: str | None = None,
) -> GraphBuildStats

compute_adjacency_stats() measures an adjacency matrix in memory (a dense array is converted to sparse); file_bytes is set when path is an existing file. load_adjacency_stats() unpickles a saved adjacency file and measures it. Neither knows which edges are word–word edges, so word_word_edges is None unless passed to compute_adjacency_stats().

from text4gcn import load_adjacency_stats

stats = load_adjacency_stats("data/R8.adjacency/ind.frequency.tfidf.R8.adj", builder="frequency.tfidf")
print(stats.summary())

docs.text:
from text4gcn.datasets import download, save_corpus, twenty_newsgroups

Helpers that write a corpus in the Text4GCN input format: two aligned UTF-8 files in one directory.

File One line per document <name>.txt the document text, on a single line <name>.meta <doc id>\t<train|test>\t<label>

Pass the same directory and name to TextPipeline(dataset_name=name, dataset_path=path).

docs.title: save_corpus
docs.text:
def save_corpus(
    path: str | os.PathLike[str],
    name: str,
    texts: Iterable[str],
    labels: Iterable[str],
    splits: Iterable[str],
) -> tuple[Path, Path]

Writes your own labelled corpus. Line breaks and tabs inside each text are collapsed to single spaces.

Parameter Type Description path str \| PathLike Output directory (created if missing). name str Dataset name: the prefix of both files. texts Iterable[str] One document per entry. labels Iterable[str] Class of each document. import pandas as pd

See 5 · Bring your own corpus for a walkthrough, including non-English text.

docs.title: download
docs.text:
def download(name: str, path: str | os.PathLike[str]) -> tuple[Path, Path]

Downloads a benchmark corpus into path (created if missing; ~ is expanded) as <name>.txt / <name>.meta. Each file is downloaded to a temporary .part file and verified against a SHA-256 checksum before it replaces <name>.txt / <name>.meta.

Returns the paths of the .txt and .meta files.

Raises ValueError for a name not in list(), or on a checksum mismatch (only the failing .part file is deleted; a .txt already verified stays); requests.HTTPError when the download fails with an HTTP error.

name Corpus Documents Train Test Classes "R8" Reuters-21578, 8 classes 7,674 5,485 2,189 8 "R52" Reuters-21578, 52 classes 9,100 6,532 2,568 52 "ohsumed" MEDLINE cardiovascular abstracts 7,400 3,357 4,043 23 "pubmed" PubMed diabetes abstracts 19,717 13,802 5,915 3 
from text4gcn import TextPipeline
from text4gcn.datasets import download

download("ohsumed", "data")
TextPipeline(dataset_name="ohsumed", dataset_path="data").execute()

text4gcn.datasets.data.list() returns the accepted names. Use the same name as dataset_name in the next steps.

Size

PubMed (19.7k documents) produces a large graph: plan for roughly (documents + words)² × 20 bytes of memory during training (see tutorial 5).

docs.text: from text4gcn import GNN, TrainingResult, Layer

docs.title: GNN
docs.text:
The main entry point for training a Graph Convolutional Network on a text dataset.

class GNN:
    def __init__(
        self,
        dataset_name: str,
        dataset_path: str | os.PathLike[str],
        log_dir: str = ".",
        builder: Builder = Builder.Tfidf,
        lr: float = 0.02,
        nhid: int = 200,
        seed: int = 1234,
        epochs: int = 200,
        dropout: float = 0.5,
        layer: Layer = Layer.GCN,
        early_stopping: int = 10,
        device: str | None = None,
        refinement_config: RefinementConfig | None = None,
        verbose: int = 1,
    ) -> None

docs.title: Parameters
docs.text: Parameter Type Default Description dataset_name str — Dataset name. Must match the prefix of .txt, .meta, and preprocessed files on disk. dataset_path str \| os.PathLike[str] — Directory containing the dataset files. log_dir str "." Directory where model checkpoints (.pth) and training plots are saved. builder Builder \| str Builder.Tfidf Adjacency strategy used to build the graph: a Builder or its string value (e.g. "embedding.word2vec"). Must match the adjacency files already on disk. lr float 0.02 Learning rate for the Adam optimiser. nhid int 200 Hidden layer dimension. seed int 1234 Random seed for PyTorch / NumPy / Python (reproducible training). epochs int 200 Maximum number of training epochs. dropout float 0.5 Dropout rate applied between GCN layers. layer Layer Layer.GCN GNN layer type. Only Layer.GCN is supported. early_stopping int 10 Stop when the validation loss rises above its mean over this many previous epochs (the TextGCN criterion); the best validation weights are restored. device str \| None None PyTorch device ("cpu", "cuda", "cuda:1", …). Detected automatically when None. refinement_config RefinementConfig \| None None Optional graph refinement applied after loading the corpus. verbose int 1 0 silent; 1 a progress bar over the epochs and a summary; 2 one line per epoch instead of the bar (for logs, CI and saved notebooks).

docs.title: Raises
docs.text:
The constructor raises:

Exception When FileNotFoundError dataset_path does not exist. ValueError Empty dataset_name, or verbose not 0, 1 or 2. TypeError An unsupported layer type is requested.

fit() raises FileNotFoundError when a previous step has not run; the message includes the command to fix it:

Missing Message names {dataset_name}.node_features/ The TextPipeline(...).execute() call. {dataset_name}.adjacency/ind.{builder}.{dataset_name}.adj The builder call that writes that file, e.g. Semantic(...).word2vec(...) for Builder.Word2Vec.

docs.title: fit()
docs.text:
def fit(self) -> TrainingResult

Runs the full pipeline: validates paths → loads corpus → applies optional refinement → trains GCN → evaluates on test set.

Saves the best checkpoint, metrics-acc.png and metrics-loss.png to log_dir. With the default verbose=1 it prints a progress bar while training, then a summary:

text4gcn · GNN("20NG4") · frequency.tfidf · cpu · seed 1234
  graph     14,537 nodes: 1,973 train · 219 validation · 1,455 test documents + 10,890 words
  model     GCN 14,537 → 200 → 4 · 2.91 M parameters · dropout 0.5 · lr 0.02
  ✓ train     52 epochs (early stop) · best epoch 50 (val_loss 1.3680, val_acc 93.2%)  (6m30s)
  ✓ test      accuracy 86.7% · macro-F1 86.2% · loss 1.2886 · 1,455 documents  (0.6 s)

                     class  precision  recall    f1  support
               alt.atheism      0.805   0.883 0.842      384
                       ...
  model     logs/20261017-000340123.pth

Diagnostics (array shapes, model structure) are logged at debug level: see Diagnostics.

Returns TrainingResult

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
Minimal:

from text4gcn import GNN

result = GNN(dataset_name="R8", dataset_path="data/").fit()
print(result.test_accuracy)

Full configuration:

from text4gcn import GNN, Builder, Layer

result = GNN(
    dataset_name="R8",
    dataset_path="data/",
    log_dir="logs/",
    builder=Builder.Tfidf,
    seed=1234,
    epochs=200,
    lr=0.02,
    nhid=200,
    dropout=0.5,
    early_stopping=10,
    device=None,         # auto-detect
).fit()

print(result)

Validation split

Reserve validation documents in preprocessing, not in GNN:

TextPipeline(dataset_name="R8", dataset_path="data/", seed=1234).execute(
    validation_ratio=0.10,
)

With graph refinement:

from text4gcn import GNN, Builder, RefinementConfig

result = GNN(
    dataset_name="R8",
    dataset_path="data/",
    builder=Builder.Tfidf,
    refinement_config=RefinementConfig(
        min_doc_freq=2,
        edge_weight_threshold=0.1,
        keep_docs=True,
    ),
).fit()

Force CPU:

result = GNN(dataset_name="R8", dataset_path="data/", device="cpu").fit()

docs.title: TrainingResult
docs.text:
from text4gcn import TrainingResult

Structured output of GNN.fit(). A frozen dataclass: its fields cannot be changed.

@dataclass(frozen=True)
class TrainingResult:
    test_accuracy: float
    test_loss: float
    model_path: str
    epochs_trained: int
    best_epoch: int
    metrics: dict[str, float]
    history: pandas.DataFrame
    report: pandas.DataFrame
    confusion_matrix: pandas.DataFrame

docs.title: Fields
docs.text: Field Type Description test_accuracy float Accuracy on the held-out test set (0–1). test_loss float Cross-entropy loss on the held-out test set. model_path str Path of the saved checkpoint (.pth) inside log_dir, holding the weights with the best validation loss. epochs_trained int Number of epochs that completed before stopping. best_epoch int Epoch with the lowest validation loss; its weights are the ones restored and saved. metrics dict Test accuracy, macro_precision, macro_recall, macro_f1, weighted_f1. history DataFrame One row per epoch (index epoch): loss, accuracy, val_loss, val_accuracy, seconds. report DataFrame Test precision, recall, f1, support per class, indexed by class name. confusion_matrix DataFrame Test confusion matrix: rows are true classes, columns predicted ones.

result = GNN(dataset_name="R8", dataset_path="data/").fit()

result                        # TrainingResult(accuracy=0.9712, macro_f1=0.9301, loss=0.0843, epochs=187, best_epoch=177, ...)
result.metrics["macro_f1"]    # 0.9301
result.history[["loss", "val_loss"]].plot()   # learning curves
result.confusion_matrix       # true × predicted, with class names

docs.text:
from text4gcn import TextGCNTrainer

The lower-level training loop that GNN.fit() runs. Use it only to train on data you prepared yourself; GNN is the supported entry point.

class TextGCNTrainer:
    def __init__(
        self,
        model,                      # model class, e.g. text4gcn.models.model.GCN
        args,                       # namespace of training settings (below)
        pre_data,                   # tuple returned by LoadData(...).load_corpus() / apply_refinement()
        report: Reporter | None = None,
        class_names: Sequence[str] | None = None,
    ) -> None

    def fit(self) -> dict

args is any object with the attributes device, max_epoch, nhid, lr, dropout (default 0.5), early_stopping, seed, dataset, log_dir and, when report is None, verbose (default 1) — e.g. a types.SimpleNamespace. fit() returns a dict with the fields of TrainingResult (TrainingResult(**trainer.fit()) builds one).

docs.title: TextPipeline
docs.text:
from text4gcn import TextPipeline

Cleans and shuffles the raw corpus, builds the vocabulary, and writes the label matrices and train / validation / test split that GNN loads. (It also writes node feature matrices for compatibility with the TextGCN file layout; the GCN itself uses one-hot node features.)

docs.title: TextPipeline
docs.text:
class TextPipeline:
    def __init__(
        self,
        dataset_name: str,
        dataset_path: str | os.PathLike[str],
        rare_count: int = 5,
        language: str = "english",
        seed: int = 1234,
        encoding: str = "utf-8",
        ascii_only: bool = True,
        verbose: int = 1,
    ) -> None

docs.title: Parameters
docs.text:
Parameter Type Default Description dataset_name str — Dataset name. Must match the .txt and .meta file prefixes. dataset_path str \| os.PathLike[str] — Directory containing the raw dataset files. Must exist at construction time. rare_count int 5 Words appearing fewer than this many times across the corpus are dropped. language str "english" Language for stop-word removal (NLTK stop-word list). seed int 1234 Random seed for document shuffle (reproducible train/test order). encoding str "utf-8" Encoding of the input .txt corpus. Use "latin1" for legacy corpora that are not valid UTF-8. Intermediate files are always UTF-8. ascii_only bool True Keep only A-Za-z0-9 when cleaning (original TextGCN). Set False for Arabic, Cyrillic, accented Latin, etc. verbose int 1 0 silent; 1 or 2 one summary line per stage.

Non-English corpus (e.g. Arabic)

TextPipeline(
    dataset_name="MyArabic",
    dataset_path="data/",
    language="arabic",   # NLTK stop-word list
    ascii_only=False,    # keep Arabic letters and diacritics
).execute()

docs.title: Raises
docs.text: Exception When ValueError Empty dataset_name, or verbose not 0, 1 or 2 (constructor). FileNotFoundError dataset_path does not exist (constructor). UnicodeDecodeError execute(): the .txt corpus is not valid in encoding; the message suggests TextPipeline(encoding=...), e.g. encoding='latin1'.

docs.title: execute()
docs.text:
def execute(
    self,
    validation_ratio: float = 0.10,
    seed: int | None = None,
) -> None

Runs the complete preprocessing pipeline. Stages execute in order:

  1. Clean — remove stop words and rare words, write to {dataset_name}.cleaned/
  2. Shuffle — randomise train/test order, write to {dataset_name}.shuffled/
  3. Prepare words — build the vocabulary and, for each word, the TF-IDF vector of its WordNet definitions (at most 1,000 features; used by Semantic.cosine_similarity())
  4. Build node features — compute x, y, tx, ty, allx, ally matrices, write to {dataset_name}.node_features/

Each stage prints one line, for example:

text4gcn · TextPipeline("20NG4") · language english · validation 10%
  ✓ clean     3,647 documents · 10,890 words kept (rare_count=5)  (1.1 s)
  ✓ shuffle   train 2,192 · test 1,455 documents (seed 1234)  (0.2 s)
  ✓ words     10,890 words · 8,941 with a WordNet definition  (5.7 s)
  ✓ features  train 1,973 · validation 219 · test 1,455 documents · 4 classes  (1.8 s)

The same lines, with a timestamp, are written to the processing log {dataset_path}/log/{dataset_name}_dataset.txt; the graph builders append theirs.

docs.title: Parameters
docs.text: Parameter Type Default Description validation_ratio float 0.10 Fraction of the training set held out for validation (DCAI 2022 / Yao et al. use 0.10). This is the only place where the validation split is set. seed int \| None None If given, replaces the instance's shuffle seed (TextPipeline(seed=…)): it is stored on the instance, so later execute() calls without seed reuse it.

docs.title: Output layout
docs.text:
After execute() the dataset directory contains:

data/
  R8.txt                     ← original input (unchanged)
  R8.meta                    ← original input (unchanged)
  R8.cleaned/
    R8.txt                   ← stop-word and rare-word filtered
  R8.shuffled/
    R8.txt                   ← shuffled corpus
    R8.meta                  ← shuffled metadata
    R8.train                 ← training document indices
    R8.test                  ← test document indices
    R8.vocab                 ← vocabulary (one word per line)
    R8.word_vectors          ← TF-IDF vectors of WordNet definitions (pickle)
  R8.node_features/
    ind.R8.x                 ← train doc feature matrix
    ind.R8.y                 ← train doc one-hot labels
    ind.R8.tx                ← test doc feature matrix
    ind.R8.ty                ← test doc one-hot labels
    ind.R8.allx              ← train + word node features
    ind.R8.ally              ← train + word node labels
  log/
    R8_dataset.txt           ← pipeline execution log

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
Basic usage:

from text4gcn import TextPipeline

TextPipeline(
    dataset_name="R8",
    dataset_path="data/",
    seed=1234,
).execute()

Custom rare-word threshold and validation split:

TextPipeline(
    dataset_name="R8",
    dataset_path="data/",
    rare_count=3,          # keep words appearing ≥ 3 times
    language="english",
    seed=1234,

    validation_ratio=0.15, # use 15% of train for validation
)

French corpus:

    dataset_name="lemonde",

    language="french",

docs.title: Input file format
docs.text:
{dataset_name}.txt — one document per line:

computer software programming algorithm data structures
natural language processing text classification neural

{dataset_name}.meta — tab-separated index split label (labels may contain spaces, not tabs):

0   train   technology
1   train   science
2   test    technology
3   test    business

Split values

train, training, and 20news-bydate-train are treated as training documents. All other values are treated as test documents.

docs.title: Graph Refinement
docs.text:
from text4gcn import RefinementConfig, apply_refinement

Graph refinement reduces the size and noise of the word-document graph before training. It filters word nodes by frequency or degree, prunes weak edges, and optionally builds per-node metadata.

docs.title: RefinementConfig
docs.text:
@dataclass
class RefinementConfig:
    # Node filters
    min_degree: float | None = None
    max_degree: float | None = None
    min_word_degree: float | None = None
    max_word_degree: float | None = None
    min_doc_freq: int | None = None
    max_doc_freq_ratio: float | None = None
    keep_docs: bool = True
    drop_word_indices: set[int] | None = None
    keep_word_indices: set[int] | None = None

    # Edge pruning
    edge_weight_threshold: float | None = None
    top_k_edges_per_node: int | None = None

    # Vocabulary and stopwords
    vocab_path: str | None = None
    stopwords: set[str] | None = None

    # Output
    build_metadata: bool = True

docs.title: Node filter fields
docs.text: Field Type Default Description min_degree float \| None None Drop any node with total weighted degree below this (word nodes only when keep_docs=True). Applied first. max_degree float \| None None Drop any node with total weighted degree above this (hub pruning; word nodes only when keep_docs=True). Applied first. min_word_degree float \| None None Drop word nodes with degree below this. max_word_degree float \| None None Drop word nodes with degree above this. min_doc_freq int \| None None Drop word nodes that appear in fewer than this many documents (equivalent to sklearn's min_df). max_doc_freq_ratio float \| None None Drop word nodes that appear in more than this fraction of documents (equivalent to max_df). keep_docs bool True When True, document nodes are never removed: every node filter, including min_degree / max_degree, applies to word nodes only. drop_word_indices set[int] \| None None Explicit set of vocabulary indices to drop. keep_word_indices set[int] \| None None When set, only these vocabulary indices are kept: it decides alone for word nodes and the other word filters are skipped. It does not override min_degree / max_degree, which apply first.

docs.title: Edge pruning fields
docs.text: Field Type Default Description edge_weight_threshold float \| None None Drop edges with weight strictly below this value — whatever weight the builder stored: TF-IDF (document–word), PMI (tfidf()), count / max count (RWF builders) or cosine similarity (cosine_similarity()). top_k_edges_per_node int \| None None Keep only the top-k heaviest edges per node. An edge survives if it is in the top-k of either endpoint, with its original weight.

docs.title: Vocabulary fields
docs.text: Field Type Default Description vocab_path str \| None None Path to vocabulary file (one word per line), used by stopwords and for NodeMetadata.word. Optional: if None, the vocabulary is read from {dataset_path}/{dataset_name}.shuffled/{dataset_name}.vocab when apply_refinement gets dataset_path and dataset_name (GNN always passes them). stopwords set[str] \| None None Set of word strings to drop. Only effective when a vocabulary is available: without vocab_path and without dataset_path / dataset_name, it silently does nothing.

docs.title: Output fields
docs.text: Field Type Default Description build_metadata bool True Whether to populate the metadata list in the refinement output; when False, info["metadata"] is None.

docs.title: apply_refinement()
docs.text:
from text4gcn import apply_refinement

def apply_refinement(
    predata: tuple,
    config: RefinementConfig,
    dataset_path: str | None = None,
    dataset_name: str | None = None,
    return_metadata: bool = False,
) -> tuple[tuple, dict | None]

Applies graph refinement to the output of LoadData.load_corpus() (text4gcn.models.utils.LoadData). Returns a new predata tuple with the same structure.

docs.title: Parameters
docs.text: Parameter Type Description predata tuple Output of load_corpus(): (adj, features, y_train, y_val, y_test, train_mask, val_mask, test_mask, train_size, test_size). config RefinementConfig Refinement configuration. dataset_path str \| None Dataset directory, used to auto-locate the vocabulary file. dataset_name str \| None Dataset name, used to auto-locate the vocabulary file. return_metadata bool If True, the second return value is a dict with "metadata" and "stats" keys.

docs.title: Returns
docs.text:
(predata_refined, info) where: - predata_refined — same tuple structure as predata, with the refined graph. - info — None if return_metadata=False; otherwise a dict with: - "metadata" — list[NodeMetadata], one entry per node in the refined graph; None when build_metadata=False. - "stats" — dict with:

Key Meaning nodes_original / nodes_refined / nodes_removed Node counts before and after node filtering. edges_before Stored edges after node filtering, before edge pruning. edges_after Stored edges after edge pruning. train_docs_kept Kept training documents (train_mask; validation documents are not counted). test_docs_kept Kept test documents.

docs.title: Raises
docs.text: Exception When ValueError All nodes (or all train/test docs) were removed by the filters.

docs.title: NodeMetadata
docs.text:
from text4gcn.graph import NodeMetadata

Metadata for a single node in the (possibly refined) graph.

@dataclass
class NodeMetadata:
    node_type: str          # 'train_doc', 'word', 'test_doc'
    original_index: int     # index in the un-refined graph
    degree: float           # weighted degree in the refined graph
    word_id: int | None = None   # vocabulary index (word nodes only)
    word: str | None = None      # word string (word nodes only, if vocab available)
    doc_id: int | None = None    # document index (doc nodes only)

For test documents, doc_id counts from 0 within the test block. NodeMetadata.to_dict() exports the fields as a plain dictionary for serialisation or Pandas ingestion.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
Basic — drop rare words and weak edges:

from text4gcn import GNN, Builder, RefinementConfig

result = GNN(
    dataset_name="R8",
    dataset_path="data/",
    builder=Builder.Tfidf,
    refinement_config=RefinementConfig(
        min_doc_freq=2,              # drop words in fewer than 2 docs
        edge_weight_threshold=0.1,   # drop very weak edges
        keep_docs=True,
    ),
).fit()

Advanced — inspect refinement stats:

from text4gcn import RefinementConfig, apply_refinement, Builder
from text4gcn.models.utils import LoadData

predata = LoadData(
    path="data/",
    dataset="R8",
    builder=Builder.Tfidf,
).load_corpus()

config = RefinementConfig(min_doc_freq=3, edge_weight_threshold=0.05)
predata_refined, info = apply_refinement(
    predata,
    config,
    dataset_path="data/",
    dataset_name="R8",
    return_metadata=True,
)

print(info["stats"])
# {'nodes_original': ..., 'nodes_refined': ..., 'nodes_removed': ..., 'edges_before': ..., 'edges_after': ..., ...}

Drop specific words by vocabulary index:

RefinementConfig(
    drop_word_indices={0, 1, 2},   # drop the first three vocab entries
    keep_docs=True,
)

String-based stopword filtering (needs a vocabulary: vocab_path, or dataset_path / dataset_name):

RefinementConfig(
    stopwords={"the", "a", "an", "is", "in"},
    vocab_path="data/R8.shuffled/R8.vocab",
)

docs.title: Choosing a Builder
docs.text: Text4GCN provides three families of adjacency builders. This guide helps you choose the right one for your use case.

docs.title: Quick comparison
docs.text:
Builder Method Speed Word–word edges Requires Frequency tfidf() Fast Positive PMI over a sliding window Nothing extra Semantic word2vec() Medium Adjacent words with similar Word2Vec vectors (trained on the corpus) Training time Semantic bert() Slow Adjacent words with similar BERT vectors text4gcn[bert]; downloads bert-base-uncased on first use Semantic cosine_similarity() Medium Words with similar WordNet definitions (English only) NLTK WordNet (TextPipeline downloads it) Syntactic dependency_parsing() Slow Words linked by a dependency relation text4gcn[syntactic] + CoreNLP jars Syntactic linguistic_inquiry() Fast Adjacent words sharing a LIWC category LIWC dictionary

Every builder also writes the same TF-IDF document–word edges.

docs.title: Frequency — TF-IDF (recommended start)
docs.text:
The TF-IDF builder is the default and the best starting point. It requires no external tools, runs quickly, and gives competitive results on standard benchmarks.

from text4gcn.builder import Frequency

stats = Frequency(dataset_name="R8", dataset_path="data/").tfidf(window_size=20)
print(stats)  # GraphBuildStats: nodes, edges(nnz), density, file size

Use when: - You are running your first experiment - Compute time is limited - The corpus uses standard vocabulary

Tune: - window_size — larger windows capture longer-range co-occurrence but increase noise. Start at 20; try 10 or 30 for short/long texts.

docs.title: Semantic — Word2Vec
docs.text:
Word2Vec trains embeddings on your corpus from scratch. Two adjacent non-stop-word words in a document are connected when the cosine similarity of their embeddings is at least threshold and their PMI is positive; the edge weight is the pair count divided by the largest pair count. Embeddings need a corpus large enough to train them.

from text4gcn.builder import Semantic

Semantic(dataset_name="R8", dataset_path="data/").word2vec(
    training_algorithm=1,   # 1 = skip-gram, 0 = CBOW
    embedding_dimension=300,
    num_epochs=20,
    threshold=0.7,
)

Use when: - You have a large corpus (≥ 10k documents) - Words have domain-specific meaning not captured by PMI - You want embeddings trained on your own data

Tune: - training_algorithm — skip-gram (1, used in the DCAI 2022 paper) is better on rare words; CBOW (0) is faster - seed / workers — with the default workers=1 the graph is reproducible for a given seed; more workers train faster but vary between runs - threshold — higher values create sparser graphs. On 20 Newsgroups (4 categories, 20 epochs) 0.95 kept 79 word–word edges, 0.7 kept 1,610 and 0.5 kept 11,127, all with the same accuracy; the default is 0.7

docs.title: Semantic — BERT
docs.text:
Like Word2Vec RWF, but each vocabulary word is embedded with a pre-trained BERT model (bert-base-uncased, the [CLS] vector of the word encoded on its own, out of sentence context) instead of a model trained on the corpus. Adjacent words in a document are linked when their cosine similarity is at least threshold and their PMI is positive.

from text4gcn.builder import Semantic

Semantic(dataset_name="R8", dataset_path="data/").bert(threshold=0.95)

Requirements

bert() needs pip install "text4gcn[bert]" and always uses bert-base-uncased. Train on its graph with GNN(..., builder=Builder.Bert).

Use when: - The corpus is too small to train useful Word2Vec embeddings

docs.title: Semantic — Cosine Similarity
docs.text:
Connects words whose WordNet definitions are similar: TextPipeline saves a TF-IDF vector of each word's WordNet glosses, and the builder links two words when the cosine similarity of those vectors exceeds the threshold. Words that WordNet does not know get no word–word edges.

English only

WordNet definitions are in English. On other languages almost no word has a definition, so the graph keeps only the document–word edges.

from text4gcn.builder import Semantic

Semantic(dataset_name="R8", dataset_path="data/").cosine_similarity(threshold=0.90)

Use when: - You want a semantic measure from a lexical resource, without training Word2Vec - The corpus is in English

docs.title: Syntactic — Dependency Parsing
docs.text:
Edges between syntactically related words (subject-verb, adjective-noun, etc.) using Stanford CoreNLP. Each dependency relation (except ROOT) between two non-stop-word words counts as a pair; like the other RWF builders, a pair needs positive PMI, and its weight is its pair count divided by the largest pair count.

from text4gcn.builder import Syntactic

Syntactic(dataset_name="R8", dataset_path="data/").dependency_parsing(
    core_nlp_path="/opt/stanford-corenlp",
    language="english",
)

Experimental

Needs pip install "text4gcn[syntactic]" and a local Stanford CoreNLP installation (Java jars), which CI does not run. CoreNLP always parses English; language selects the NLTK stop-word list whose words get no edges.

Use when: - Formal text where grammatical relations carry classification signal - Linguistic analysis is the goal

docs.title: Syntactic — LIWC
docs.text:
Connects adjacent words that share at least one LIWC (Linguistic Inquiry and Word Count) psycholinguistic category (e.g. "positive emotion", "cognitive process"). Like the other RWF builders, a pair needs positive PMI, and its weight is its pair count divided by the largest pair count.

from text4gcn.builder import Syntactic

Syntactic(dataset_name="R8", dataset_path="data/").linguistic_inquiry(
    liwc_path="data/LIWC2015.dic",
)

Use when: - Sentiment, affect, or psychological framing is relevant to the classification task - You already have a LIWC dictionary licence

docs.title: Mixing builders
docs.text:
Each builder writes a separate adjacency file. You can build multiple adjacency matrices and train separate GNN models to compare:

from text4gcn.builder import Frequency, Semantic
from text4gcn import GNN, Builder

dataset_name = "R8"
dataset_path = "data/"

Frequency(dataset_name=dataset_name, dataset_path=dataset_path).tfidf()
Semantic(dataset_name=dataset_name, dataset_path=dataset_path).word2vec(
    training_algorithm=1, embedding_dimension=300, num_epochs=20
)

result_tfidf = GNN(dataset_name=dataset_name, dataset_path=dataset_path, builder=Builder.Tfidf).fit()
result_w2v   = GNN(dataset_name=dataset_name, dataset_path=dataset_path, builder=Builder.Word2Vec).fit()

print(f"TF-IDF:   {result_tfidf.test_accuracy:.4f}")
print(f"Word2Vec: {result_w2v.test_accuracy:.4f}")

docs.title: Builder ↔ GNN.builder enum mapping
docs.text:
When calling GNN, pass the builder that matches the adjacency file you built:

from text4gcn import GNN, Builder

GNN(..., builder=Builder.Tfidf)           # reads ind.frequency.tfidf.R8.adj
GNN(..., builder=Builder.Word2Vec)        # reads ind.embedding.word2vec.R8.adj
GNN(..., builder=Builder.Bert)            # reads ind.embedding.bert.R8.adj
GNN(..., builder=Builder.CosineSimilarity) # reads ind.cosine.similarity.R8.adj
GNN(..., builder=Builder.DependencyParsing) # reads ind.dependency.parsing.R8.adj
GNN(..., builder=Builder.Liwc)            # reads ind.liwc.R8.adj

docs.title: Device Management
docs.text: Text4GCN uses PyTorch and trains on CPU or on an NVIDIA GPU (CUDA). Device selection is automatic by default.

docs.title: Automatic detection
docs.text:
When device=None (the default), GNN uses CUDA if torch.cuda.is_available(), and the CPU otherwise.

from text4gcn import GNN

result = GNN(dataset_name="R8", dataset_path="data/").fit()
# Automatically uses CUDA if available

docs.title: Manual device selection
docs.text:
Override the device with the device parameter:

# Force CPU
result = GNN(dataset_name="R8", dataset_path="data/", device="cpu").fit()

# Specific CUDA device
result = GNN(dataset_name="R8", dataset_path="data/", device="cuda:1").fit()

Any PyTorch device string is passed on as is. Devices other than cpu and cuda, such as Apple's mps, are never selected automatically and are not tested.

docs.title: Checking your PyTorch installation
docs.text:
from text4gcn.utils.device import check_pytorch_installation

info = check_pytorch_installation()
print(info)
# {'torch_version': '2.3.0', 'cuda_available': True, 'cuda_version': '12.1'}

docs.title: Installation by hardware
docs.text:
pip install text4gcn installs PyTorch from PyPI. On Linux that build already supports CUDA; on Windows and macOS it is CPU-only.

To choose the build yourself, for example a specific CUDA version, or a CPU-only build on Linux (a much smaller download), install PyTorch first with the command from pytorch.org, then Text4GCN:

pip install torch --index-url https://download.pytorch.org/whl/cpu   # example: CPU-only
pip install text4gcn

docs.title: Performance notes
docs.text:
The GCN trains on the whole graph at once, with the normalised adjacency held as a dense matrix: memory grows with the square of the number of nodes (documents + vocabulary words). On 20 Newsgroups with 4 categories (14.5k nodes), one training run took about 7 minutes on CPU. See tutorial 5 to estimate the memory of your own corpus before training.

Graph building (Frequency.tfidf() and the other builders) always runs on the CPU; a GPU speeds up only the training.

docs.title: Multi-GPU
docs.text: Multi-GPU training is not currently supported. Use device="cuda:N" to select a specific GPU when multiple are available.

docs.title: Graph Refinement
docs.text:
Graph refinement reduces the word-document graph before training — removing low-quality word nodes and pruning weak edges. This can reduce training time, decrease overfitting, and sometimes improve accuracy.

For the full API reference see RefinementConfig.

docs.title: When to use refinement
docs.text:
Symptom Suggested filter Training is slow due to large graph min_doc_freq, edge_weight_threshold Common function words dominate features stopwords, max_doc_freq_ratio Sparse long-tail words add noise min_doc_freq, min_word_degree Hub nodes distort neighbourhood aggregation max_word_degree, top_k_edges_per_node

Refinement is optional. The default TextPipeline already applies rare_count filtering; refinement lets you apply additional graph-level constraints without re-running the pipeline.

docs.title: Applying refinement via GNN
docs.text:
The simplest way is to pass a RefinementConfig to GNN. Refinement is applied after loading the corpus, before training.

from text4gcn import GNN, Builder, RefinementConfig

result = GNN(
    dataset_name="R8",
    dataset_path="data/",
    builder=Builder.Tfidf,
    refinement_config=RefinementConfig(
        min_doc_freq=2,              # drop words in fewer than 2 docs
        edge_weight_threshold=0.1,   # drop very weak edges
        keep_docs=True,              # never remove document nodes
    ),
).fit()

docs.title: Dropping rare words
docs.text:
RefinementConfig(min_doc_freq=2)

Drops word nodes that appear in fewer than 2 documents. Equivalent to min_df=2 in scikit-learn vectorisers.

RefinementConfig(min_doc_freq=5, max_doc_freq_ratio=0.90)

Also drops words that appear in more than 90% of documents (equivalent to max_df=0.90).

docs.title: Dropping by node degree
docs.text:
RefinementConfig(min_word_degree=1.0)

Drops word nodes whose weighted degree (the sum of their edge weights) is below 1.0, including isolated words.

RefinementConfig(max_word_degree=5000.0)

Drops hub word nodes with degree above 5000 — extremely connected words that dilute neighbourhood information.

RefinementConfig(min_degree=1.0, max_degree=5000.0)

Same test on every node's weighted degree. With keep_docs=True (default) document nodes are exempt, so it only drops words; with keep_docs=False it can drop documents too.

docs.title: Edge pruning
docs.text:
RefinementConfig(edge_weight_threshold=0.05)

Removes all edges whose stored weight is below 0.05 — whatever the builder stored: TF-IDF for word–document edges; PMI (tfidf()), count / max count (RWF builders) or cosine similarity (cosine_similarity()) for word–word edges.

RefinementConfig(top_k_edges_per_node=10)

Keeps only the 10 heaviest edges per node. Creates a sparser, cleaner graph. An edge survives if it is among the 10 heaviest of either endpoint, and keeps its original weight.

docs.title: Stopword filtering
docs.text:
RefinementConfig(
    stopwords={"the", "a", "an", "is", "in", "of", "to"},
    vocab_path="data/R8.shuffled/R8.vocab",
)

Drops word nodes for any word in stopwords. The vocabulary maps word strings to vocabulary indices: vocab_path is optional — when it is None, the vocabulary is read from <dataset_path>/<dataset_name>.shuffled/<dataset_name>.vocab. GNN always passes dataset_path and dataset_name; with apply_refinement, pass them (or vocab_path) yourself, otherwise stopwords silently does nothing.

docs.title: Drop / keep by vocabulary index
docs.text:
RefinementConfig(drop_word_indices={0, 1, 5, 100})
RefinementConfig(keep_word_indices={10, 20, 30})  # whitelist; all others dropped

keep_word_indices decides alone for word nodes: the other word filters are ignored. min_degree / max_degree still apply first.

docs.title: Always keep document nodes
docs.text:
RefinementConfig(keep_docs=True)  # default

When True, document nodes (train and test) are never removed regardless of other filters. Set to False only if you have a specific reason to filter documents.

docs.title: Combining filters
docs.text:
All filters are applied together. Order of application:

  1. Global degree filters (min_degree, max_degree)
  2. Whitelist (keep_word_indices) — if set, it alone decides which word nodes stay and steps 3–6 are skipped
  3. Word-only degree filters (min_word_degree, max_word_degree)
  4. Document frequency filters (min_doc_freq, max_doc_freq_ratio)
  5. Index filter (drop_word_indices)
  6. Stopword filter (stopwords)
  7. Edge pruning (edge_weight_threshold, top_k_edges_per_node), on the graph left after node filtering

Document nodes pass all node filters when keep_docs=True.

docs.title: Inspecting refinement statistics
docs.text:
Use apply_refinement directly with return_metadata=True to see what was removed:

from text4gcn import RefinementConfig, apply_refinement, Builder
from text4gcn.models.utils import LoadData

predata = LoadData(
    path="data/",
    dataset="R8",
    builder=Builder.Tfidf,
).load_corpus()

config = RefinementConfig(
    min_doc_freq=3,
    edge_weight_threshold=0.05,
    keep_docs=True,
)
predata_refined, info = apply_refinement(
    predata, config, dataset_path="data/", dataset_name="R8", return_metadata=True
)

stats = info["stats"]
print(f"Nodes: {stats['nodes_original']} → {stats['nodes_refined']} ({stats['nodes_removed']} removed)")
print(f"Edges: {stats['edges_before']} → {stats['edges_after']}")

edges_before counts the edges left after node filtering, before edge pruning; edges_after counts them after pruning.

info["metadata"] holds one NodeMetadata per kept node (type, original index, degree, word or document id). Pass build_metadata=False to skip it; info["metadata"] is then None.

docs.title: Complete example
docs.text:
from text4gcn import GNN, Builder, RefinementConfig

result = GNN(
    dataset_name="R8",
    dataset_path="data/",
    builder=Builder.Tfidf,
    epochs=200,
    early_stopping=10,
    refinement_config=RefinementConfig(
        min_doc_freq=2,
        max_doc_freq_ratio=0.85,
        edge_weight_threshold=0.05,
        top_k_edges_per_node=20,
        keep_docs=True,
    ),
).fit()

print(f"Accuracy: {result.test_accuracy:.4f}")

docs.title: Understanding the Text Graph
docs.text: Text4GCN represents a corpus as a heterogeneous word-document graph. This page explains the graph structure and why it is effective for text classification.

docs.title: Node types
docs.text:
The graph contains two kinds of nodes:

Node type Count Represents Document nodes train_size + test_size One node per document in the corpus Word nodes vocab_size One node per unique word in the vocabulary

After preprocessing, the nodes are ordered as:

[train_doc_0, ..., train_doc_{n-1},  word_0, ..., word_{V-1},  test_doc_0, ..., test_doc_{m-1}]

docs.title: Edge types
docs.text:
Edge Direction Weight Meaning Word ↔ Word Undirected Depends on the builder (PMI for tfidf()) Two words are related Word ↔ Document Undirected TF-IDF score A word appears in a document with that importance

There are no document-document edges in the default graph (documents only connect through shared words).

Every builder writes the same TF-IDF word–document edges; they differ only in the word–word edges:

Builder Word–word weight Frequency.tfidf() PMI over a sliding window (below) Semantic.word2vec(), Semantic.bert(), Syntactic.linguistic_inquiry(), Syntactic.dependency_parsing() (RWF) Pair count divided by the largest pair count; positive PMI is only a gate Semantic.cosine_similarity() Cosine similarity of the two word vectors

See Graph builders.

docs.title: Word-word edges (PMI)
docs.text:
For Frequency.tfidf(), Pointwise Mutual Information is computed over a sliding window of size window_size:

PMI(w_i, w_j) = log( p(w_i, w_j) / (p(w_i) * p(w_j)) )

Only positive PMI values produce an edge.

docs.title: Word-document edges (TF-IDF)
docs.text:
TF-IDF measures how important a word is to a specific document relative to the whole corpus:

TF-IDF(w, d) = tf(w, d) * log(N / df(w))

where tf(w, d) is the term frequency in document d, N is the number of documents, and df(w) is the number of documents containing w.

docs.title: Why a graph?
docs.text:
Bag-of-words models (TF-IDF vectors, naive Bayes) treat words independently. A graph captures co-occurrence context: if "neural" and "network" always appear together, the graph creates a strong edge between them and the model can leverage that signal.

GCNs propagate information along edges. A document node aggregates information from its word nodes; word nodes aggregate from both documents and co-occurring words. After two GCN layers, each document node contains a summary of:

  1. Its own word content (layer 1)
  2. Words that those words co-occur with (layer 2)

This is richer than a bag-of-words embedding with no structural signal.

docs.title: Graph size
docs.text:
For a corpus with D documents and vocabulary size V:

Quantity Size Nodes D + V Word-doc edges up to D × V (sparse in practice) Word-word edges up to V × V; depends on the builder (and on window_size for PMI)

For the R8 benchmark, the DCAI 2022 paper reports 7,674 documents and 7,688 words after filtering, so 15,362 nodes, and about 3.2 M edges in the TextGCN graph: word–word PMI edges dominate.

docs.title: Inspecting the graph
docs.text:
After building adjacency with Frequency(...).tfidf(), the matrix is saved as a pickled scipy.sparse matrix. You can load and inspect it directly:

import pickle, scipy.sparse as sp

with open("data/R8.adjacency/ind.frequency.tfidf.R8.adj", "rb") as f:
    adj = pickle.load(f)

print(adj.shape)   # (nodes, nodes): training docs, then words, then test docs
print(adj.nnz)     # stored entries; GNN makes the graph symmetric when loading it

Or load the corpus and pass it through apply_refinement with return_metadata=True to get per-node type and degree information:

from text4gcn import Builder, RefinementConfig, apply_refinement
from text4gcn.models.utils import LoadData

predata = LoadData(path="data/", dataset="R8", builder=Builder.Tfidf).load_corpus()
_, info = apply_refinement(
    predata, RefinementConfig(), dataset_path="data/", dataset_name="R8", return_metadata=True
)

node = info["metadata"][0]   # one NodeMetadata per node
print(node.node_type, node.degree)
print(info["stats"])
# {'nodes_original': …, 'nodes_refined': …, 'nodes_removed': 0, ...}

An empty RefinementConfig() removes nothing; info["metadata"] is None when build_metadata=False.

docs.title: Tutorials
docs.text:
Five notebooks that take you from "what is a text graph?" to training on your own corpus. Each one answers the question the previous one leaves open, so they read best in order.

flowchart LR
    A["1 · Text as a graph<br/><small>what the graph is</small>"] --> B["2 · Your first classifier<br/><small>raw text → accuracy</small>"]
    B --> C["3 · Choosing a graph builder<br/><small>which edges?</small>"]
    C --> D["4 · Refining the graph<br/><small>fewer edges, same accuracy?</small>"]
    D --> E["5 · Bring your own corpus<br/><small>your data, any language</small>"]
# Tutorial You will learn Runtime 1 Text as a graph What nodes and edges Text4GCN builds, and why an unlabelled document can be classified from its place in the graph seconds, CPU 2 Your first classifier The full pipeline on the 20 Newsgroups benchmark: download, TextPipeline, Frequency.tfidf(), GNN.fit() ~2.5 min GPU 3 Choosing a graph builder TF-IDF + PMI vs. Word2Vec RWF vs. cosine similarity: edges, build time and accuracy side by side ~4.5 min GPU 4 Refining the graph Measuring and pruning a built graph with RefinementConfig, and what it does to accuracy ~2.5 min GPU 5 Bring your own corpus From a DataFrame to the input files, non-English text, encodings and memory sizing seconds, CPU

docs.title: The story in one paragraph
docs.text: TextGCN turns a corpus into one graph of documents and words and lets a GCN pass labels along its edges (1). On a real benchmark that graph classifies well, but it has millions of edges (2). The Related Word Filter of Pereira & de Castro (DCAI 2022) connects only related words and keeps comparable accuracy with an order of magnitude fewer edges, because the document–word edges carry most of the signal (3). Refinement prunes an existing graph further, without rebuilding it (4). Everything carries over to your own data and language (5).

def force_layout(linked: np.ndarray, steps: int = 300, seed: int = 0) -> np.ndarray:
    """Fruchterman-Reingold: linked nodes attract, every pair of nodes repels."""
    xy = np.random.default_rng(seed).normal(size=(len(linked), 2))
    k = 1 / np.sqrt(len(linked))
    for step in np.linspace(0.1, 0.002, steps):
        delta = xy[:, None] - xy[None, :]
        dist = np.linalg.norm(delta, axis=-1) + 1e-9
        force = ((k**2 / dist**2 - linked * dist / k)[..., None] * delta).sum(axis=1)
        length = np.linalg.norm(force, axis=1, keepdims=True) + 1e-9
        xy += force / length * np.minimum(length, step)
    return xy

def remove_overlaps(xy: np.ndarray, radius: np.ndarray, steps: int = 300) -> np.ndarray:
    """Nudge apart every pair of nodes closer than the sum of their radii."""
    for _ in range(steps):
        delta = xy[:, None] - xy[None, :]
        dist = np.linalg.norm(delta, axis=-1) + np.eye(len(xy))
        overlap = np.clip(radius[:, None] + radius[None, :] - dist, 0, None) * (1 - np.eye(len(xy)))
        xy = xy + 0.25 * ((overlap / dist)[..., None] * delta).sum(axis=1)
    return xy

def node_label(k: int) -> str | None:
    """Topic of node k if it is a document (test labels are used only for colouring)."""
    kind = nodes.kind.iloc[k]
    return None if kind == "word" else meta.label.iloc[k if kind == "train doc" else k - n_words]

A GCN learns how much each hop and each feature should count, instead of using fixed weights. Because test documents are nodes of the same graph, the model is transductive: classifying a new document means adding it to the graph and training again.
