docs.title: 1 · Text as a graph¶
docs.text:
A bag-of-words classifier looks at each document on its own. TextGCN (Yao et al., 2019) takes a different view. The whole corpus becomes one graph, whose nodes are the documents and the words, and a Graph Convolutional Network learns by passing information along its edges.

Before training anything on a real dataset, we build that graph for twelve sentences and open it up. By the end you will know what nodes and edges Text4GCN creates, and why an unlabelled document can be classified just from its position in the graph.

Runs on CPU in a few seconds.

# Tutorial Question it answers 1 Text as a graph What does the graph look like, and why does it help? 2 Your first classifier How do I go from raw text to test accuracy? 3 Choosing a graph builder How should words be connected? 4 Refining the graph Can a smaller graph do as well? 5 Bring your own corpus How do I use my own (non-English) data?

docs.title: A tiny corpus¶
docs.text:
Two topics, space and cooking, with five labelled training sentences each. The two test sentences have labels too, but the model will never see them: we only use them to check the predictions at the end.

save_corpus writes the two files Text4GCN reads: toy.txt, with one document per line, and toy.meta, with <id>\t<train|test>\t<label>.

docs.title: Step 1: preprocess¶
docs.text: TextPipeline lower-cases and tokenizes the text and removes stop words. It also drops words seen fewer than rare_count times; with twelve sentences we keep every word, so rare_count=1. It then shuffles the documents and saves the vocabulary.

docs.title: Step 2: build the graph¶
docs.text: Frequency.tfidf() builds the original TextGCN graph and saves its adjacency matrix, a scipy.sparse matrix, with pickle. It returns GraphBuildStats, whose path field points to that file.

docs.title: Who is who¶
docs.text:
The adjacency matrix is square: one row per node. The nodes are in a fixed order:

[ training documents | vocabulary words | test documents ]

docs.title: Two kinds of edges¶
docs.text:
• word–word: two words that co-occur in the same sliding window more often than chance. The weight is their PMI (pointwise mutual information).
  • document–word: a word that occurs in a document. The weight is its TF-IDF.

There are no document–document edges. Documents only meet through shared words.

docs.title: Seeing the structure¶
docs.text:
We draw the graph with a small force-directed layout: edges pull their nodes together, and all nodes push each other apart. Nothing here has been trained, and labels are used only for the colours.

Each coloured circle is a document (D7 is document 7), each beige circle a word. A word grows with its number of edges, so the words shared by several documents stand out. Test documents are drawn hollow: the model never sees their label.

docs.title: Zooming in: two hops from a test document¶
docs.text: The full drawing hides the edge weights. Let's zoom in on the first test document, "The chef baked fresh bread and served it with soup": its words, and the training documents that share at least one of them. These are exactly the nodes two hops away, the ones a 2-layer GCN mixes into its prediction.

docs.title: The same graph as a matrix¶
docs.text: The GCN never sees a drawing. It sees the adjacency matrix $A$, where $A_{ij}$ is the weight of the edge between nodes $i$ and $j$, or zero if there is none. Rows and columns follow the node order above, so the matrix splits into blocks:

docs.title: Why this helps: labels travel along edges¶
docs.text:
A 2-layer GCN computes

$$\hat{A} \cdot \mathrm{ReLU}(\hat{A} \cdot X \cdot W_1) \cdot W_2, \qquad \hat{A} = D^{-1/2} (A + I) \, D^{-1/2}$$

where $X$ holds the node features and $W_1$, $W_2$ are the learned weights. $\hat{A}$ is the normalised adjacency: self-loops are added ($A + I$), and every weight is divided by the square root of the weighted degrees $D$ of its two nodes. Every layer mixes each node with its neighbours, so after two layers a document has heard from its words and from the other documents that share those words.

docs.title: 2 · Your first classifier¶
docs.text:
In tutorial 1 we built a graph of twelve sentences. Now we use the 20 Newsgroups benchmark (one of the datasets of Yao et al., 2019 and Pereira & de Castro, DCAI 2022) and go all the way to test accuracy:

  1. Download it and write the Text4GCN input files.
  2. Preprocess it with TextPipeline.
  3. Build the graph with Frequency.tfidf().
  4. Train and evaluate a GCN with GNN.fit().

Runtime: with the 4-category subset (~3.6k documents) this takes about 2.5 min on a T4 GPU and needs about 4 GB of RAM. Almost all of it is building the graph (about 2 min), which runs on the CPU; a GPU speeds up only the training, which takes several times longer on CPU.

# Tutorial Question it answers 1 Text as a graph What does the graph look like, and why does it help? 2 Your first classifier How do I go from raw text to test accuracy? 3 Choosing a graph builder How should words be connected? 4 Refining the graph Can a smaller graph do as well? 5 Bring your own corpus How do I use my own (non-English) data?

docs.title: Configuration¶
docs.text: The whole corpus, documents and vocabulary, becomes a single graph. The full 20NG (18,846 posts) therefore needs a large GPU. We use the four categories of the classic scikit-learn text tutorial. To scale up, add categories or set CATEGORIES = None.

docs.title: 1. Download and write the input files¶
docs.text:
twenty_newsgroups() downloads the corpus with scikit-learn (already a dependency) and keeps the official train/test split. It strips e-mail headers, signatures and quoted replies, so the model learns from the message body, and it drops posts left with fewer than 5 words. It then calls save_corpus(), which writes the two files every Text4GCN dataset needs:

| File | One line per document | |---|---| | <name>.txt | the text, on a single line | | <name>.meta | <doc id>\t<train|test>\t<label> |

We start from an empty folder: TextPipeline rewrites its own files, but outputs left by an older run, such as a graph built for another vocabulary, would stay next to them.

docs.title: 2. Preprocess¶
docs.text:
execute() writes three folders next to the input files:

Folder Content <name>.cleaned/ text lower-cased and tokenized, without stop words and words seen fewer than rare_count times <name>.shuffled/ documents shuffled with seed, the vocabulary, the train/test ids <name>.node_features/ feature and label matrices; validation_ratio of the training documents is held out for validation

validation_ratio is the only place where the validation split is defined.

docs.title: 3. Build the graph¶
docs.text: The TextGCN graph has PMI word–word edges and TF-IDF document–word edges (see tutorial 1). GraphBuildStats reports its size.

docs.title: 4. Train and evaluate¶
docs.text: GNN loads the features and the graph and trains a 2-layer GCN with the protocol of the paper: hidden size 200, dropout 0.5 and learning rate 0.02. Training stops early when the validation loss rises above its mean over the previous 10 epochs (the criterion of the reference TextGCN code). It uses CUDA when available. When training stops, the weights with the best validation loss are restored and evaluated on the test documents.

docs.title: What's next¶
docs.text:
The graph above has millions of edges, most of them word–word PMI pairs. Do we need all of them?

docs.title: 3 · Choosing a graph builder¶
docs.text:
The TextGCN graph of tutorial 2 connects two words whenever they co-occur more often than chance. That gives millions of edges: most of the memory and most of the build time.

The Related Word Filter (RWF) of Pereira & de Castro (DCAI 2022) asks a simple question: what if only related words were connected? The semantic variant trains Word2Vec on the corpus. It keeps a word–word edge only when the two embeddings are very similar, and keeps the TF-IDF document–word edges unchanged.

Here we build three graphs on the same preprocessed corpus, train the same GCN on each and compare them.

Runtime: about 4.5 min on a T4 GPU, almost all of it building the TF-IDF + PMI and Word2Vec RWF graphs (about 2 min each). Graph building runs on the CPU; a GPU speeds up only the training, which takes several times longer on CPU.

# Tutorial Question it answers 1 Text as a graph What does the graph look like, and why does it help? 2 Your first classifier How do I go from raw text to test accuracy? 3 Choosing a graph builder How should words be connected? 4 Refining the graph Can a smaller graph do as well? 5 Bring your own corpus How do I use my own (non-English) data?

docs.title: Three ways to connect words¶
docs.text:
Graph Word–word edges Builder TF-IDF + PMI (TextGCN) positive PMI over a sliding window Builder.Tfidf Word2Vec RWF (DCAI 2022) adjacent words whose corpus-trained Word2Vec embeddings have cosine similarity $\geq$ threshold, and positive PMI Builder.Word2Vec Cosine similarity words whose WordNet definitions are similar: cosine of the TF-IDF vectors of their glosses $>$ threshold Builder.CosineSimilarity

All three keep the same TF-IDF document–word edges, so the graphs differ only in their word–word edges. Each builder writes its own adjacency file, and GNN(builder=...) selects which one to train on.

docs.title: Reading the results¶
docs.text:
On our GPU run (seed 1234):

  • The Word2Vec RWF graph had $16\times$ fewer edges (0.28 M vs 4.5 M), a 3.3 MiB file instead of 52 MiB, and took about the same time to build (~2 min: 1m47s vs 2m07s). It lost about one point of accuracy (85.6% vs 86.7%). This is the trade-off reported in the DCAI 2022 paper: much smaller graphs with comparable accuracy.
  • The word–word column shows where the difference lies (each word–word edge is stored in both directions). The PMI of TextGCN adds 4.3 M word–word entries. The RWF keeps 3,220 and the cosine graph 17,290: both graphs are almost entirely made of the TF-IDF document–word edges.
  • The RWF and cosine graphs differ by only about 0.4 points (85.6% vs 85.2%), and both are only 1–1.5 points below TextGCN's 86.7%, with $16\times$ fewer edges. Their weights explain part of it: an RWF edge weighs its pair count divided by the largest pair count, so it is at most 1 and usually much lighter than a TF-IDF document–word edge.

On this corpus the document–word edges carry most of the signal. The 4.3 M PMI edges buy about one point of accuracy; the RWF and cosine word–word edges change graph size a lot and accuracy only slightly.

Which one to choose:

  • Start with TF-IDF + PMI. It is the TextGCN baseline and the most accurate here.
  • Use Word2Vec RWF when memory matters: about one point less for a $16\times$ smaller graph.
  • threshold sets the size of the RWF graph. Measure accuracy on your own data before tuning it.
  • The cosine graph compares WordNet definitions, so it is meaningful for English only.
  • The syntactic graphs (Syntactic.dependency_parsing(), Syntactic.linguistic_inquiry()) follow the same pattern but need a local Stanford CoreNLP installation or a LIWC dictionary; dependency_parsing() is marked experimental. See the builders guide.

Next: the builder decides which edges exist. 4 · Refining the graph prunes an existing graph instead, without rebuilding it.

docs.title: 4 · Refining the graph¶
docs.text:
Tutorial 3 showed that a graph with far fewer edges can classify almost as well. Choosing a builder is one way to get there. Graph refinement is another: it takes a graph that is already built and removes rare words and weak edges before training, without rebuilding anything.

We first measure what each refinement removes, which takes seconds and needs no training. Then we train on a few of the refined graphs.

Runtime: about 2.5 min on a T4 GPU, almost all of it building the TF-IDF graph (about 2 min). Graph building runs on the CPU; a GPU speeds up only the training of the four models, which takes several times longer on CPU.

docs.title: The knobs¶
docs.text:
RefinementConfig combines node filters and edge pruning. Document nodes are always kept (keep_docs=True), so the train, validation and test sets do not change.

Option Removes min_doc_freq=k words that occur in fewer than $k$ documents max_doc_freq_ratio=r words that occur in more than a fraction $r$ of the documents edge_weight_threshold=w edges with a PMI or TF-IDF weight below $w$ top_k_edges_per_node=k all but the $k$ heaviest edges of each node

See the refinement guide for the full list.

docs.title: Measure before you train¶
docs.text: LoadData(...).load_corpus() loads the graph and features that GNN would train on. apply_refinement(..., return_metadata=True) returns the refined graph together with statistics, without training.

docs.title: Does accuracy survive?¶
docs.text: We train on the original graph and on three refined ones. GNN applies the refinement after loading the graph and prints the same statistics as above.

docs.title: What the numbers say¶
docs.text:
On our GPU run (seed 1234):

  • min_doc_freq=3 removed about 600 rare words and lost almost nothing (86.6% vs 86.7%). Fewer nodes means less memory, because the dense GCN grows with the square of the node count.
  • Dropping the weaker half of the edges (keeping $w \geq$ median) cost only about 0.3 points (86.3%). Moderate pruning is safe.
  • top-20 edges/node kept only 8% of the edges, but accuracy dropped by about 3.6 points (83.0%).
  • Compare that with tutorial 3: counted as here (document–word edges in both directions), the Word2Vec RWF graph has about 556 k entries, 12% of the 4.8 M (its builder reports 279,559 of 4,534,779 edges, about 6%), and it lost only about 1 point.

The difference is which edges go. top-k treats all edges alike, so documents with more than 20 words lose document–word edges. The RWF removes word–word edges only and keeps every document–word edge, and tutorial 3 showed that on this corpus those edges carry most of the signal.

docs.title: Takeaways¶
docs.text:
• Measure first. Graph statistics take seconds; training takes minutes.
  • Prune words, not just edges. min_doc_freq is a safe first step.
  • For an order-of-magnitude smaller graph, change the builder (tutorial 3) rather than pruning TF-IDF + PMI.
  • Keep the document–word edges. Filters that remove them, like top-k, cost the most accuracy.
  • Refinement works with any builder: pass refinement_config together with builder.

Next: so far we have used a benchmark. 5 · Bring your own corpus shows how to prepare your own data, in any language.

docs.title: 5 · Bring your own corpus¶
docs.text:
Every tutorial so far has started from a benchmark. Your data probably lives in a CSV file or a DataFrame, and it may not be in English. This tutorial covers the checklist for using your own corpus:

  1. Format: from a DataFrame to .txt + .meta with save_corpus().
  2. Language: stop words and non-ASCII scripts.
  3. Encoding: files that are not UTF-8.
  4. Size: will the graph fit in memory?

We use a small Portuguese corpus written inline. Runs on CPU in a few seconds.

# Tutorial Question it answers 1 Text as a graph What does the graph look like, and why does it help? 2 Your first classifier How do I go from raw text to test accuracy? 3 Choosing a graph builder How should words be connected? 4 Refining the graph Can a smaller graph do as well? 5 Bring your own corpus How do I use my own (non-English) data?

docs.title: 1. From a DataFrame to Text4GCN files¶
docs.text: A typical labelled dataset has a text column and a label column, and either a split column or no split at all. If there is no split, create one with scikit-learn and stratify it, so that every class appears in both train and test.

docs.title: 2. Language: stop words and non-ASCII text¶
docs.text:
Two TextPipeline options matter for languages other than English:

  • language: the NLTK stop-word list to remove, for example "portuguese", "spanish" or "arabic".
  • ascii_only: the original TextGCN cleaning keeps only A-Za-z0-9. That breaks accented words (clássico becomes cl ssico) and erases scripts such as Arabic completely. Set ascii_only=False to keep letters of any script.

Compare the vocabulary produced by each setting:

docs.title: 3. Encoding¶
docs.text: TextPipeline reads the corpus as UTF-8 by default. Older datasets are often Latin-1 or Windows-1252. In that case reading fails with a message telling you to pass the encoding, for example TextPipeline(..., encoding="latin1"). encoding applies to the .txt file; the .meta file must always be UTF-8. save_corpus always writes UTF-8, so data that went through it is safe.

docs.title: 4. Will the graph fit?¶
docs.text: The graph has one node per document plus one per vocabulary word. During training, the normalised adjacency and the identity node features are both kept as dense $N \times N$ matrices, $N$ being the number of nodes. Peak memory therefore grows with the square of the node count. We measured about 20 bytes per pair of nodes (3.9 GiB for the 14.5k-node graph of tutorial 2):
